To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
human H ferritins and R. catesbianna ferritins have a different number and pattern of iron-binding sites that precede their OS and that this is reflected in their different catalytic activity.

the iron path in human heavy-chain ferritins is more complex and less efficient than in the amphibian R. catesbienna ferritin, and that the differences between the two proteins are due to the presence of additional transient iron-binding sites that define the path to the OS.

the crystal structures of iron-bound human ferritin reveal multiple iron-binding sites that define the iron pathway to the oxidoreduc-tase sites and that these structures provide the first direct experimental evidence for the existence of reaction intermediates along this pathway.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of transient iron binding sites in human ferritin and their role in iron biomineralisation.
the elucidation of the iron binding and storage mechanism in human H ferritin.

the identification of the iron path in ferritin and its role in the iron biomineralizing activity of the protein, with the aim of providing a structural and mechanistic basis for the design of new iron-storage proteins for biotechnological applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the different pattern of iron sites in H ferritin and R. catesbiana ferritin are the result of the different iron oxidation pathways that occur in the two proteins.
the iron-binding sites of ferritin are not just passive storage sites but are involved in the iron-binding process.

iron binding to human H ferritin is more efficient than that to M ferritin from R. catesbiena, and the reason for this difference is that the human H protein has a higher density of transient iron-binding intermediates than the frog protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the iron-binding sites of the human H ferritin have a more complex pattern compared with the R. catesbienna counterpart.

the iron-binding sites in ferritin, and the iron path from entry channels to OS, have a high degree of conservation across the species, but that the ligands that define these sites are not conserved, and this is reflected in differences in the kinetics of iron binding and release.
the iron binding and oxidation pathway of human H ferritin differs from that of R. catesbienna M ferritin, which is likely to have an impact on the activity of the two ferritin proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the OS is a complex site that can be accessed through a number of different routes that involve a number of different intermediates, and the different patterns of iron-binding sites in different ferritins are likely to be a reflection of the different iron-binding properties of these proteins.

iron binding to ferritin is a highly dynamic process that is not only dictated by the cage architecture of the protein but also by the nature of the iron sites and their interactions with the protein matrix.
the OS is not a static site, and the transient binding of iron to the OS is a crucial step in the biomineralization process.
